inline.s: [If in a single thought you press through, then all deluded thoughts fall away at once, like the shadow of a flower in empty space falling, like the waves of a mirage growing clear. Once past this pass, you gain measureless ease and lightness, measureless freedom. This is where the beginner first gains strength; it is nothing mysterious. Yet when ease and lightness come, you must not give rise to a joyful mind. If you give rise to a joyful mind, the joy-demon takes hold of your mind, and one more obstruction is added.]

If in a single thought you press through, then all deluded thoughts fall away at once, like the shadow of a flower in empty space fading, like the waves of a mirage growing clear. Once past this pass, you gain measureless ease and lightness, measureless freedom. This is where the beginner first gains strength; it must not be regarded as something mysterious. As for ease and lightness, again you must not give rise to a joyful mind. If you give rise to a joyful mind, the joy-demon takes hold of your mind, and one more obstruction is added.

[Flower in empty space] For one whose eyes are diseased, a flower is seen in empty space; but empty space has no flower at all — it is merely the false seeing of diseased eyes. This is a metaphor for illusion. “Flower” (huā) is the ancient form of “flower” (huā). [Mirage] A vapor that arises under the blazing sun; from afar it looks like water, and the thirsty deer longs to drink, but in the end it cannot be obtained. It is a metaphor for illusion, and is one of the ten similes of the Mahāyāna. [Beginner] One who has just brought forth the mind to learn the Buddhadharma.

[As for the seeds of habitual tendencies and the roots of craving in the storehouse consciousness, they are firm and lie deep. Where the huatou can find no strength, where the contemplation of mind cannot reach, where you yourself cannot lay your hand — there you must bow to the Buddha, recite sutras, and repent, and again secretly uphold the mantra-heart, relying on the Buddha’s secret seal to dispel them. For all the secret mantras are the Buddha’s adamantine mind-seal. When we use them, it is like holding the adamantine vajra scepter: it shatters every thing, and whatever thing it meets becomes dust. The mind-seal and secret key of all the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old are nowhere beyond this. Hence it is said: “The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-heart, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.” Yet the Buddha spoke of it openly; the patriarchs’ gate, fearing that it would fall into the ordinary sentiments of men, kept it secret and did not speak of it — not that they did not use it. This requires a fixed daily lesson; when it has long been practiced until thoroughly familiar, the strength gained is very great. Only you must not hope for miraculous responses.]

As for the seeds of habitual tendencies and the roots of craving in the storehouse (ālaya) consciousness, they are firm and lie deep. At this point the huatou yields no strength, the contemplation of mind cannot illumine, and you yourself cannot lay your hand to it. Then you must bow to the Buddha, recite sutras, and repent, and again secretly uphold the mantra-heart, relying on the Buddha’s secret seal to dispel them. For all the secret mantras are the Buddha’s adamantine mind-seal. When we recite the mantra-heart, it is like holding the adamantine vajra scepter: whatever it meets, it shatters into dust. The mind-seal and secret key of all the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times are nowhere beyond this. Hence it is said: “The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-heart, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.” Yet the Buddha spoke it openly to teach living beings; the patriarchs’ gate, fearing that it would fall into the ordinary sentiments of men, kept it secret and did not speak of it — not that they did not use it. Upholding the mantra-heart in secret requires a fixed daily lesson; when it has long been practiced until thoroughly familiar, the strength gained is very great, but you must not hope for miraculous responses.

[Mantra-heart] The essential and vital part of all mantras. In the Surangama Sutra, after the Buddha had spoken the Surangama Mantra, he called it the mantra-heart. The sutra says: “The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of this mantra-heart, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and universal enlightenment. … The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-heart, can in the ten directions lay their hands upon the crown and bestow the prediction of enlightenment.”

[Among those who cultivate, there are some who awaken first and then cultivate, and some who cultivate first and then awaken; but awakening has the difference of understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. If one clarifies the mind by relying on the teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs, that is understanding-awakening; it mostly falls into knowledge and views, and in all states and conditions it mostly finds no strength. For mind and state stand opposed and cannot merge; wherever one turns one is blocked, and many obstructions arise. This is called semblance prajñā, not true investigation. As for one who realizes and awakens, he works plainly and honestly onward from within his own mind, pressing on to the place where the waters run out and the mountains end, until suddenly a single thought comes to rest in an instant, and he comprehends his own mind through and through, as plainly as meeting one’s own father at the crossroads — there is no longer any doubt. Like a man drinking water, who alone knows for himself whether it is cold or warm, and cannot pour it out for another. This is true investigation and real awakening. Thereafter, with the place of his awakening he merges mind and state, and purifies the manifest karmic outflowing consciousness; deluded thoughts and emotional calculations are all smelted into a single-flavored true mind. This is realization-awakening.]

Among those who cultivate, there are some who awaken first and then cultivate (sudden awakening, gradual cultivation), and some who cultivate first and then awaken (gradual cultivation, sudden awakening); hence awakening has understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. If one clarifies the mind by relying on the teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs, that is understanding-awakening. One who has understanding-awakening mostly falls into knowledge and views, and in all states and conditions mostly finds no strength. This is because mind and state still stand opposed and have not merged; hence, meeting states and conditions, one is entangled by them, and many obstructions arise. This is semblance prajñā, not true investigation. As for one who realizes and awakens, he works plainly and honestly onward from within his own mind (carrying on the work of contemplating mind or investigating Chan), pressing on to the place where the waters run out and the mountains end, until suddenly a single thought (a subtle thought) comes to rest in an instant, and he comprehends his own mind through and through, as plainly as meeting one’s own father at the crossroads — recognized at a glance, with no doubt whether it is he or not. Of such a state it is said, like a man drinking water, that only he himself knows whether it is cold or warm, and there is no way to tell another. Only this is true investigation and real awakening. Thereafter, with the place of his awakening he merges mind and state, purifies the manifest karmic outflowing consciousness, and smelts deluded thoughts and emotional calculations wholly into a single-flavored true mind. This is realization-awakening.

This passage says: Chan practice has two roads, sudden awakening with gradual cultivation and gradual cultivation with sudden awakening, and the meaning of their awakening (seeing the nature) differs accordingly. The awakening of sudden awakening with gradual cultivation is understanding-awakening; the awakening of gradual cultivation with sudden awakening is realization-awakening. The Prefaces to the Collected Interpretations of the Sources of Chan says: “If one cultivates because of awakening, that is understanding-awakening; if one awakens because of cultivation, that is realization-awakening.”
[This realization-awakening also has differences of depth. If one works from the root, breaks through the old rut of the eight consciousnesses
(kē jiù)

, and in an instant overturns the den of ignorance, leaping straight in with nothing left over — this is the sharpest of the sharp, and what he realizes is deep. The rest, who cultivate gradually, realize what is shallow. Above all, fear being content with little; above all, avoid falling into the doorway of light and shadow. Why? Because the root of the eight consciousnesses is not yet broken; whatever one does is all on the side of the spirit of consciousness. If one takes this for the real, it is much like taking a thief for one’s son. The ancients said: “The student of the Way does not know the real, for from former times he has known only the spirit of consciousness; the root of birth and death through measureless kalpas, the fool takes for the original person.” This one pass above all must be gotten through.]

This realization-awakening also has differences of depth. If one works from the root (working purely and simply upon the single thought alone), breaks through the old rut of the eight consciousnesses, in an instant overturns the den of ignorance, and leaps straight in with nothing left over — this is a person of the sharpest of the sharp faculties, and what he realizes is deep. The rest, who cultivate gradually, realize what is shallow. What is most to be feared is being content with little; above all, avoid falling into the doorway of light and shadow and taking it for the ultimate, making no further advance. Why is this? Because the root ignorance of the eight consciousnesses is not yet broken; though one may accomplish something, it is all on the side of the spirit of consciousness (the knowing mind). If one takes this for the real, it is just like taking a thief for one’s son. The ancients said: “The student of the Way does not know the real, for from former times he has known only the spirit of consciousness; the root of birth and death through measureless kalpas (the root of birth and death), the fool takes for the original person.” This one pass of falling into the doorway of light and shadow must by all means be gotten through.

[Breaking through the old rut of the eight consciousnesses] Breaking through the old set pattern by which the eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and ālaya-consciousness) give rise to mind in dependence on objects — this is the state of great awakening. “Old rut” (kē jiù) means a ready-made pattern, an old set way.

[Root ignorance] Also called beginningless ignorance: from beginningless time the self-nature, with a single thought of non-awakening, has lain in the long night of confusion, not understanding the truth, and can give rise to all delusions and afflictions.

[Taking a thief for one’s son] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Suppose there is a man who takes a thief for his son; the family treasure will never be secured.” [Spirit of consciousness] The knowing mind. The knowing mind is also called the mind of conditioning — the mind that climbs upon the six dusts and arises.

[As for what is called sudden awakening with gradual cultivation: it is that one has first awakened thoroughly, but still has habitual tendencies that cannot be purified at once. So in all states and conditions, with the principle one has awakened to, one raises the power of contemplation, testing the mind through states as they come. Merge one part of state and you realize one part of dharma-body. Dissolve one part of deluded thought and you manifest one part of fundamental wisdom. This again lies wholly in close and continuous work, done upon states and conditions, where it gains even more strength.]

As for what is called sudden awakening with gradual cultivation: it is that one has first awakened thoroughly, but still has habitual tendencies that cannot be purified at once. So in all states and conditions, with the principle one has awakened to, one raises the power of contemplation, testing the mind through states as they come. Merge one part of state and you realize one part of dharma-body. Dissolve one part of deluded thought and you manifest one part of fundamental wisdom. This again is done wholly by close and continuous work upon states and conditions, and so gains even more strength.

[Fundamental wisdom] That is, root wisdom, also called undiscriminating wisdom: the true wisdom by which the Buddhas and bodhisattvas personally realize suchness and accord with the true character of all dharmas.

[Among those of sharp faculties whose faith is fierce, who in cultivation are willing to do the work, the obstruction of things is easily removed, but the obstruction of principle is hard to dispel. Of the disease-energies here, I will briefly set out one or two.]

All those of sharp faculties and fierce faith are willing to take pains in their cultivation; the obstruction of things is easily removed, but the obstruction of principle is hard to dispel. Of the disease-energies here, I will briefly set out one or two below.

[Obstruction of things and obstruction of principle] Afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion can keep birth and death continuous and obstruct great nirvāṇa, and are called the “obstruction of things”; wrong views can hinder right knowledge and vision and obstruct great bodhi, and are called the “obstruction of principle.”

[First, do not greedily seek the mysterious and profound. For this matter is from the first plain and even, solid and down-to-earth, wholly ordinary, with nothing mysterious about it at all. Hence the ancients said: “Awakened, one is still the same as before awakening — still the same person as of old, though no longer treading the old path.” There is nothing mysterious whatsoever. When the work arrives, it is naturally plain and real. But because our habit of intellectual understanding is not yet pure, it inwardly perfumes the prajñā. The prajñā, perfumed by that habit, gives rise to illusions, produces many clever views, wraps them close about the mind, and one supposes this to be the mysterious and profound, clinging to it deeply and unwilling to let go. This is precisely the shadowy brightness of the spirit of consciousness, the root of discriminating false views, also called the thorn of views. Unlike the coarse, floating deluded thoughts that came before, this is the subtle flowing stream of arising and ceasing; it is also called the obstruction of knowledge, and it is precisely what obstructs right knowledge and vision. If one takes it for the real, all sorts of wild views arise. This is what must above all be avoided.]

First, do not greedily seek the mysterious and profound. For this matter is from the first plain and even, solid and down-to-earth, wholly ordinary, with nothing mysterious about it at all. Hence the ancients said: “Awakened, one is still the same as before awakening — still the same person as of old (not increased by a hair’s breadth), yet no longer treading the old path (after awakening the eye is bright as snow, no longer deceived by seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing; hence in meeting states and conditions one handles them differently than before, no longer clinging to appearances).” Therefore there is nothing mysterious about it. If the work is brought to maturity, it is naturally plain and real. But because our habit of intellectual understanding is not yet pure, it inwardly perfumes the prajñā. The prajñā, perfumed by the habit of intellectual understanding, is measured and weighed by the feelings of consciousness, and so gives rise to many illusions and produces all kinds of false, profound-seeming views; these wrap and bind the mind, yet one takes them for the mysterious and profound, and clings to them deeply, unwilling to let go. How could one know that this is precisely the shadowy brightness of the spirit of consciousness, the root of discriminating false views, also called the thorn of views? It differs from the earlier coarse and superficial deluded thoughts; this is the subtle flowing stream of arising and ceasing, also called the obstruction of knowledge, and it is precisely what obstructs right knowledge and vision. If one mistakes it and takes it for a true state, all manner of arrogant views arise. This is what cultivation most forbids.

[Second, do not set the mind to wait for awakening. For our wondrous, perfect, true mind is from the first free of all duality. Previously, because deluded thoughts congealed, mind and state, faculties and dusts, stood opposed to one another, and so delusion arose and karma was made. Now the cultivator should simply take a single thought. Put down body, mind, and world, and take up this single thought alone and go forward; by no means mind whether you are awakened or not — just go on doing it thought by thought, step by step. When the work reaches its place, you will of yourself see your original face; why reckon it in advance? If you set the mind to wait for awakening, this very waiting mind is the root of birth and death. Wait until the kalpa is exhausted, and still you cannot awaken. For you do not understand the true mind that is free of all duality, and suppose there is something else. If the waiting mind is not removed, weariness easily arises, and one mostly falls back. It is like searching for a lost thing and not finding it, and so giving rise to the thought of giving up.]

Second, do not set the mind to wait for awakening. For our wondrous, perfect, true mind is from the first free of all duality. Previously, because deluded thoughts congealed, mind and state, faculties and dusts, stood opposed to one another, and so delusion arose and karma was made. Now in cultivation one should simply work upon the single thought. Put down body, mind, and world, and take up this single thought alone (contemplating mind or investigating Chan) and go forward; by no means mind whether you are awakened or not — just go on doing it thought by thought, step by step. If the work reaches its place, you will of yourself see your original face; why reckon it in advance? If you set the mind to wait for awakening, this very mind of waiting for awakening is the root of birth and death. Wait until the year of the donkey and the month of the horse, and still you cannot awaken. This is because you do not understand the true mind that is free of all duality, and suppose there is something else. If the waiting mind is not removed, weariness easily arises, and one mostly falls back. It is like searching for a lost thing and not finding it, and so giving rise to the thought of giving up.

[Free of all duality] Beyond all opposites. Duality means the two sides standing opposed, as black and white, great and small, good and evil, and so on. To be free of duality is that true suchness is equal and without discrimination, and no dharma is obtainable; hence it is beyond all opposites, and is briefly called being free of duality. It is synonymous with the absolute.

[Third, do not seek the wondrous fruit. For the deluded mind of birth and death in living beings is originally the Tathāgata’s fruit-essence. Now, in the midst of delusion, one turns the Buddhas’ spiritual penetrations and wondrous functions into deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, into discriminating knowledge and views; turns the true and pure dharma-body into the substance of karmic birth and death; turns the pure and wondrous land into the states of the six dusts. Now, in doing the work, if a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind, it is like a great smelting furnace casting all things. This very body, mind, and world are originally the Tathāgata’s fruit-essence; this very deluded thought and emotional calculation is originally spiritual penetration and wondrous function; the name changes, but not the substance. Yongjia says: “The real nature of ignorance is precisely the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is precisely the dharma-body.” If one can awaken to this Dharma gate, then the feelings of grasping and rejecting are forgotten, the mind of delight and aversion comes to rest, and every step is the Pure Land of the Flower Treasury, every thought the descent of Maitreya. If one settles the mind first upon seeking the wondrous fruit, this very seeking mind is the root of birth and death, and obstructs right knowledge and vision. The more one seeks, the farther away it is; when the strength of seeking is exhausted, weariness arises.]

Third, do not seek the wondrous fruit. For the deluded mind of birth and death in living beings is originally the Tathāgata’s fruit-essence. (When the self-nature is deluded, one is a living being; when the self-nature is awake, one is a Buddha.) Now, with the self-nature in delusion, one turns the Buddhas’ spiritual penetrations and wondrous functions into deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, into discriminating knowledge and views; turns the true and pure dharma-body into the substance of karmic birth and death; turns the pure and wondrous land into the states of the six dusts. Now, in doing the work, if a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind, it is like the great crimson furnace of the Creator casting all things. This very body, mind, and world are originally the Tathāgata’s fruit-essence; this very deluded thought and emotional calculation is originally spiritual penetration and wondrous function; the name changes, but not the substance. As Great Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “The real nature of ignorance is precisely the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is precisely the dharma-body.” If one can awaken to this Dharma gate, then the feeling of grasping and rejecting is forgotten, the mind of delight and aversion comes to rest, and every step is the Pure Land of the Flower Treasury, every thought the descent of Maitreya (the attainment of Buddhahood). If one first settles the mind upon desiring the wondrous fruit, then this seeking mind is the root of birth and death, and obstructs right knowledge and vision. The more one seeks the wondrous fruit, the farther one is from realizing the Way; and seeking without obtaining, one’s strength is exhausted and weariness arises.
[Great smelting furnace] A metaphor for the Creator.

[Fourth, do not give rise to doubts of your own. Whenever one does the work, one should throughout put down body and mind and shut off seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing. Having left one’s former steps behind, one gazes ahead into the vast and
(ancient form of miao, “remote and dim”)
dim, with no place to settle the body and establish the life.

Fourth, do not give rise to doubts of your own. Whenever one does the work, once one has put down body and mind and shut off seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, one has left the familiar old road behind; gazing ahead on the new road, it is strange and dim, with no place to settle the body and establish the life. Advancing, there is no new realization; retreating, one loses one’s former dwelling. In such a case, if one schemes and worries over before and after, doubt arises. Then measureless calculations spring up, and one weighs gain and loss. Or one gives rise to subjective opinions and sets loose wrong thoughts, obstructing right knowledge and vision. This one must be seen through, and then one will resolutely enter straight ahead, with no further misgiving. Generally speaking, when the work is done to the point where it can be done no further, that is precisely where it gains strength; one should rouse one’s spirit the more and go on, and so will not fall back. Otherwise, one falls into the demon of sorrow.
[Spirit (jīngcǎi)] Countenance; vigor.

[Fifth, do not give rise to a mind of terror. It means that when the thought-power of the work is urgent, pressing the deluded thoughts until a single thought comes to rest in an instant, suddenly body and mind fall away into emptiness, and one sees that the great earth has not an inch of soil, profound beyond the utmost — and then great terror arises. If one does not see through this, one dares not go forward. Or one takes this expansive emptiness for something excellent and wondrous. If one takes this emptiness as real, one gives rise to the great wrong view of denying cause and effect; in this lies the greatest danger.]

Fifth, do not give rise to a mind of terror. When the thought-power of the work is urgent, pressing the deluded thoughts until a single thought comes to rest in an instant, suddenly body and mind fall away into emptiness, and one sees that the great earth has not an inch of soil, profound beyond the utmost — then great terror arises. If one does not see through such a state, one dares not go forward. Or one takes this expansive emptiness (the emptiness of all things) for an excellent and wondrous state. If one takes this emptiness for an excellent and wondrous state, one gives rise to the great wrong view, no longer believing in cause and effect; this is the most dangerous of all the passes.
[Denying cause and effect] Negating cause and effect. “Denying” (bō) means casting away. The Surangama Sutra says: “Denying cause and effect, one falls wholly into emptiness.”

[Sixth, resolve to believe that your own mind is Buddha. For the Buddha has no other Buddha; only mind is. Since the Buddha’s true dharma-body is like empty space, if one understands that delusion is originally empty, the originally possessed dharma-body of itself appears, luminous and still, perfect and all-pervading, lacking nothing and with nothing left over. Do not again let the mind race outward in search. If you abandon this mind and seek elsewhere, then within the mind all sorts of measureless dreamlike states will arise. These are precisely the transformations of the spirit of consciousness; by no means take them for something extraordinary. For in our pure mind there is originally not a single thing, and not a single thought. Whenever a thought arises or moves, one departs from the dharma-substance.]

Sixth, resolve to believe that your own mind is Buddha. For the Buddha has no other Buddha; one’s own mind is. Because the Buddha’s true dharma-body is like empty space, if one realizes that deluded thoughts are originally empty and false, the originally possessed dharma-body of itself appears, luminous and still, perfect and all-pervading, lacking nothing and with nothing left over. Do not again let the mind race outward in search. If you abandon this mind and seek elsewhere, then within the mind all sorts of measureless dreamlike states will appear. These are precisely the transformations of the spirit of consciousness; by no means take them for something extraordinary. You should know that in our pure mind there is originally not a single thing, and not a single thought. Whenever a thought arises or moves, one departs from the dharma-substance.

[Seventh, you must know that deluded thoughts are originally empty and false. Those who do the work today simply do not know that the deluded thoughts of their own minds are originally empty and false. They mistake these deluded thoughts for the real and devote themselves only to opposing them. It is like a child playing with the shadows of a lamp: the more he plays, the less they have to do with anything, and after playing long he grows frightened of them himself. There is another sort who fear deluded thoughts, and wish they could seize them in one grasp and fling them aside. This is like catching the wind and snatching at shadows: all day long one wrestles with them, exhausts one’s strength, and never has a single thought of rest. Entangled thus day after day, one’s faith grows daily wearier. One says only that the investigation of Chan has no efficacy, and so gives rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of falling back — this is the common disease of beginners. There is no other cause: it is simply that one does not understand the permanently abiding true mind, the nature that is unborn and undying, but takes deluded thought for a real dharma. Here you must by all means get through; if you would pass this pass, there is of itself a road that goes beyond.]

Seventh, you must know that deluded thoughts are originally empty and false. Those who do the work today simply do not know that the deluded thoughts of their own minds are originally empty and false. They mistake these deluded thoughts for the real and devote themselves only to opposing them. It is like a child playing with the shadows of a lamp: the more he plays, the less they have to do with anything, and after playing long he grows frightened of them himself. (This means: if one mistakes deluded thoughts for the real and sets oneself against them, it is like a child playing with his own shadow on the wall — not only are the deluded thoughts not put to rest, but the more he plays the stranger they grow, and after long playing he takes them for a demon and is terrified.) There is another sort who fear deluded thoughts, and wish they could seize them in one grasp and fling them aside. This is like catching the wind and snatching at shadows: all day long one wrestles with them, exhausts one’s strength, and never has a single thought of rest. Entangled thus day after day, one’s faith grows daily wearier. One says only that the investigation of Chan has no efficacy, and so gives rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of falling back — this is the common disease of beginners. There is no other cause: it is all because one has not understood the permanently abiding true mind, which is unborn and undying, but takes deluded thought for a real dharma. Here you must by all means get through; if you can pass this pass, there is of itself a road that goes beyond.

[Eighth, you need only investigate apart from mind, consciousness, and perception, and seek apart from the realm of deluded thoughts. Whenever a single thought arises, whether it be good or evil, put it aside at once; by no means set yourself against it. Truly believe that in your own mind there was originally no such thing; merely take up your root huatou and raise it with all your strength, like the adamantine sword of the vajra king, which cuts down both demons and Buddhas. Here what is most needed is great courage, great vigor, and great patience. By no means calculate before and after; by no means be faint-hearted. Only gain a straightforward mind and right thought, straighten your back and go forward, and you will of yourself be lofty and magnificent, no longer entangled by such deluded thoughts, like a hawk slipped from its jesses. Throughout the six periods of the day, in all states and conditions, you will of yourself be unhindered, and will of yourself gain great ease and lightness and great freedom. This is where the beginner’s first step of the work gains strength.]

Eighth, you need only investigate apart from mind, consciousness, and perception, and seek apart from the realm of deluded thoughts. Whenever a single thought arises, whether it be good or evil, put it aside at once; by no means set yourself against it. Truly believe that in your own mind there was originally no such thing; merely take up your root huatou and raise it with all your strength, like the adamantine sword of the vajra king — when a demon (an evil thought) comes, the demon is cut down; when a Buddha (a good thought) comes, the Buddha is cut down. Here what is most needed is great courage, great vigor, and great endurance. By no means calculate before and after; by no means be faint-hearted and hesitant. Only gain a straightforward mind and right thought, straighten your back and go forward, and you will of yourself be lofty and magnificent, no longer entangled by these deluded thoughts, like a hawk slipped from its jesses, flying free. Throughout the six periods of the day, in all states and conditions, you will of yourself be unhindered, and will of yourself gain great ease and lightness and great freedom. This is where the beginner’s first step of the work gains strength.

[Mind, consciousness, and perception] Mind refers to the eighth consciousness (ālaya-consciousness), perception to the seventh consciousness (manas), and consciousness to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). [A hawk slipped from its jesses] Like a hawk whose leg-cords have been untied, freeing it from the leather sleeve — a metaphor for no longer being bound. Jesses (gōu)
gōu
were the leather sleeve worn on the arm when shooting with the bow in ancient times.

[The several points above are much like drawing legs on a snake; they are but words of expedience for a time. They are not ultimate, nor are they a real dharma. For having set foot on the road and taken one step out of the gate, I feared you might fall into a diverging bypath, waste your mind and strength, and vainly lose your time. You must by all means take a true and single gate that transcends, the wondrous adorned road. Then it is as said: walking is level and even, and its speed is like the wind; and the ground one treads can make a day and a kalpa change places. In short, the Buddhas’ and patriarchs’ road that goes beyond does not involve stages or a journey; yet in the beginner’s expedient means, one must get through right here before it can be had.]

The several points spoken above are much like drawing legs on a snake; they are merely words of expedience for a time. They are not ultimate, nor are they a real dharma. Because you have already set out on the road, I feared only that this one step out of the gate might be taken wrongly, so that you would stray into a bypath, waste your mind and strength, and vainly lose your time; hence I had no choice but to say all this. In cultivation one must take a true road to Buddhahood (the wondrous adorned road of the single gate that transcends). If the road is right and the method is right (walking level and even, its speed like the wind), then progress is swift — what would have taken a whole kalpa is now reached in a single day. In short, the Buddhas’ and patriarchs’ road that goes beyond does not require walking any great distance or spending any great length of time before one can realize the fruit. At the first step of a beginner, one must understand this principle before it can be done.

[The wondrous adorned road of the single gate that transcends] The Surangama Sutra says: “At that time the World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, stretched out his golden arm and laid his hand upon Ananda’s crown, and told Ananda and the whole great assembly: There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Surangama King, complete in the ten thousand practices, the wondrous adorned road by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.” The full title of the Surangama Sutra is “The Great Buddha-Crown Sutra of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Ultimate Meaning of Cultivation and Realization, and the Ten Thousand Practices of the Bodhisattvas.” [Surangama] The name of the samādhi attained by the Buddha. [Walking] Treading. [The Buddhas’ and patriarchs’ road that goes beyond does not involve stages or a journey] The Essentials of the Transmission of Mind says: “Yet the realization of this mind may be slow or swift. There are those who hear the Dharma and in a single thought attain no-mind; those who attain no-mind only at the ten faiths, ten dwellings, ten practices, and ten dedications; and those who attain no-mind only at the ten grounds. Whether long or short, having attained no-mind, one abides there, and there is nothing further to cultivate or realize. Truly there is nothing to be attained, truly and not falsely. One who attains it in a single thought and one who attains it at the tenth ground: their function is exactly equal, with no difference of depth; it is only that the latter passes through kalpas and suffers hardship to no purpose.”

blocks.text: 7. The Mind-Seal of the West’s Coming

inline.s: (From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to Xiao Xuanpu, Senior Official)

[To enter the Way, one must first awaken to the fact that the mind-substance of the person at hand is originally luminous and vast, containing all and excluding nothing, utterly full and pure. Sages and ordinary beings are not established in it, and it is not confined or obstructed by body, mind, or world. This is the road that goes beyond, the mind-seal of the West’s coming; there is nothing else but this.]

To enter the Way, one must first awaken to one’s own mind-substance: originally luminous and vast, containing all and excluding nothing, utterly full and pure. Sages and ordinary beings are not established in it, and it is not confined or obstructed by body, mind, or world. This is the road that goes beyond, the mind-seal of Patriarch Bodhidharma’s coming from the West; there is nothing else but this.

[The mind-seal of the West’s coming] The Garden of the Ancestral Court says: “Bodhidharma came from the West, established nothing in words, and single-mindedly transmitted the mind-seal, pointing directly at the human mind, so that one sees the nature and becomes Buddha.” [Mind-seal] Also called the “Buddha mind-seal.” The Buddha’s own inner realization is called the Buddha mind. The truth he realized is like a seal in the world, and so it is called the mind-seal.

[If one can awaken thoroughly to this mind, then in daily use and in meeting conditions, all states are like images in a mirror: coming, they leave no sticking; going, they leave no trace. Thus all that one does flows out from the true mind and true reality, and each thing is a work that is true and undecaying. It not only vies in brightness with the sun and moon; compared with the petty workings of deluded men’s deluded thoughts and contrivances, how can it be spoken of in the same breath?]

If one can awaken thoroughly to this mind, then in daily use and in meeting conditions, all states are like images in a mirror: coming, they leave no sticking; going, they leave no trace. Thus all that one does flows out from the true mind and true reality, and each thing is a true and undecaying work. It not only vies in brightness with the sun and moon; compared with the petty workings of deluded men’s deluded thoughts and contrivances, how can it be spoken of in the same breath?

[This radiance is complete in everyone, originally without lack. But because the view of self is firm, whatever one does one must count as one’s own achievement, and one holds one’s own views to be certainly right, so that right and wrong cross and tangle, and in the end there is no settled conclusion. The reason is this: without a mind vast and utterly impartial, to wish to build a work undecaying for a thousand autumns is hard indeed.]

The radiance of one’s own mind-substance is complete in everyone, originally without lack (the same as “deficiency”). But because the view of self is firm, whatever one does one must count as one’s own achievement, and one obstinately holds one’s own views to be certainly right, so that right and wrong cross and tangle, and in the end there is no settled conclusion. The reason is this: without a mind vast and utterly impartial, to wish to build a work undecaying for a thousand autumns is very hard to accomplish.

[Our mind-substance is originally perfect and luminous. That we cannot now awaken suddenly, and cannot enjoy it here and now, is because through measureless kalpas greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, and all kinds of affliction, have obstructed and covered our own minds. Hence the work of gradual cultivation cannot be dispensed with. Weishan says: If a student can in a single thought suddenly awaken to his own mind, he need only take what he has awakened to and purify the manifest karmic outflowing consciousness — this is called cultivation. It is not that apart from this there is some other cultivation.]

Our mind-substance is originally perfect and luminous. That we cannot now awaken suddenly, and cannot enjoy it here and now, is because through measureless kalpas greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, and all kinds of affliction, have obstructed and covered our own minds. Hence the work of gradual cultivation cannot be dispensed with. Weishan (the first patriarch of the Weiyang school) says: If a student of the Way can in a single thought suddenly awaken to his own mind, he need only take what he has awakened to and purify the manifest karmic outflowing consciousness — this is called cultivation. It is not that apart from this there is some other cultivation.

[If a student of the Way seeks only sudden awakening and thinks that is the end of it, supposing there is no work to be done, then his habitual tendencies lie deep and secretly, and meeting states they steal forth; in time he flows into the realm of demons. Yet the work of gradual cultivation has no fixed stages either. Only in daily use, at the place where thought has not yet arisen or moved, plant your feet firmly and turn the light back to illumine within. Wherever a thought arises, at once pursue and examine that thought: from where does it arise? Pursue it to the place where the single thought is born, and it is originally unborn; then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations melt like ice on the spot. What must be guarded against is lack of courage: unable to seize the throat, one does not notice the continuity, and so flows on without returning.]

If a student of the Way seeks only sudden awakening and takes it that the great matter is finished and no further cultivation is needed, then the habitual tendencies of beginningless kalpas lie deeply hidden in the ālaya-consciousness, and meeting states they secretly break out; in time he flows into the realm of demons. Therefore, after sudden awakening, one must cultivate gradually. Yet in doing the work of gradual cultivation there is no fixed sequence either. Only in daily life, at the place where thought has not yet arisen or moved, plant your feet firmly and turn the light back to illumine within. Whenever a thought arises, at once pursue and examine that thought: from where does it arise? Pursue it to the place where the single thought is born, and it is originally unborn; then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations melt like ice on the spot. But what must be feared is lacking courage: unable to seize the throat (the vital point, the place where the thought arises), one loses awareness and lets deluded thoughts continue, and so sinks into deluded thoughts without being able to pull free.

[Realm of demons] Also called the way of demons. The Treatise on the Perfection of Great Wisdom says: “It snatches away the life of wisdom and destroys the roots of Dharma-practice, merit, and goodness; therefore it is called a demon.” [The place where a thought arises] The moment a single thought first arises.

Question: I too have grasped the “turning the light back to illumine within” that Master Hanshan speaks of, and know it is a wondrous method of cultivation; but I have tried it very many times and still cannot lay my hand to it. What should I do?

Answer: The “preliminary” stage of the “Awareness of Buddha-Recitation” and “Awareness Chan” courses in the “Practice as Taught” practical curriculum is the common foundation of Buddha-recitation, mind-contemplation, and Chan investigation. First cultivate according to the “preliminary” section; when the work of “awareness of thoughts” is already deep, you may begin to cultivate this wondrous method.
Question: The method of “turning the light back to illumine within” is used here for gradual cultivation after sudden awakening. I have not yet awakened; may I cultivate according to this method?

Answer: You may. Bring this work to the point where a single thought suddenly comes to rest, and you see your original face through and through — that is realization-awakening. This is the road of gradual cultivation with sudden awakening.
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to Zhou Ziyin)

[Your letter seeking instruction is most sincere and earnest. But in what concerns the two words “empty” and “illusory,” you have not grasped them precisely, and so with regard to mind and states you are not without obstruction, and hence your work is hard to do. Now I will point them out for you, and then you will be clear and free of all doubt.]

Your letter seeking instruction is most sincere and earnest. But in what concerns the meaning of the two words “empty” and “illusory,” you have not yet understood them truly, and so with regard to mind and states you are not without obstruction, and hence your work is hard to do. Now I will point them out for you, and then all will be clear, and you will have no further doubt.

[What is called “empty” is not the emptiness of utter non-existence; it is just like the common saying “as if no one were beside one” — does that mean there is really no one beside one? It is only that, raising one’s eyes, one does not see that person. What is called “illusory” is not the illusion of strange transformations, but means having something yet not being real. It is like the peep-show in the marketplace, conjuring up all sorts of figures. Yet in that box there was originally nothing, and suddenly there they are; though they appear, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are originally nothing; and because they are originally nothing, we speak of “empty.” Hence it is said: for example, a magically created person — it is not that there is no magically created person, but that a magically created person is not a real person. Since the person is not real, is this not empty? The Buddha’s word “empty” is meant to break the worldly man’s attachment to things as truly existing; it is not the sense of utter non-existence and annihilation. Truly fearing that worldly men would sink into annihilation, he further spoke the word “illusory” to dispel that view of annihilation. Thus all body, mind, and dharmas: because of illusion they are empty, and because of emptiness they are spoken of as illusory.]

What is called “empty” is not the emptiness of utter non-existence; it is just like the common saying “as if no one were beside one” — where is it that there is really no one beside one? It is only that one thinks oneself so grand that one does not see others. What is called “illusory” is not the illusion of strange transformations, but means having something yet not being real. It is like the peep-show on the street, in which all sorts of figures suddenly appear. Yet in that box there was originally nothing, and suddenly there they are; though they appear, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are originally nothing; and because they are originally nothing, we speak of “empty.” Hence it is said: for example, a magically created person — it is not that there is no magically created person, but that a magically created person is not a real person. Since the person is not real, is this not “empty”? The Buddha’s word “empty” is meant to break the worldly man’s attachment to all dharmas as truly existing; it is not to say that all dharmas are utterly non-existent and annihilated. Yet again, fearing that worldly men would take “empty” to mean “empty of all things” and so sink into annihilation, he further spoke the word “illusory” to dispel that view of annihilation. Therefore all body, mind, and dharmas: because of illusion they are said to be empty, and because of emptiness they are said to be illusory.

[Peep-show] Within a wooden box are placed scrolls of painted pictures, and on the top of the box is a row of small round holes (three or four of them), with magnifying lenses set in the holes. After the customer pays, he puts his eye to a hole and looks inside. Then the box’s owner slowly turns a handle at the side of the box, and picture after picture passes continuously before the viewer’s eyes. Usually the pictures tell story after story. [The Buddha’s word “empty”] In the Buddhadharma, that which has appearance but no substance (as things in a dream) is called “empty,” that is, an illusion. The Buddha’s word “empty” is meant to break the worldly man’s inverted thought that falsely clings to all dharmas as truly existing. In the Sutra of Upholding the World, the Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like an illusion without reality, having no root.” In describing the existence of things, besides “existence” and “non-existence” there is another case, namely illusion, as things in a dream: having appearance but no substance, not truly existing. The concept “empty” is used to describe this.
The Vimalakirti Sutra·

, Chapter Three, “The Disciples,” says: “All dharmas are ultimately without anything whatsoever — this is the meaning of emptiness.” In this sentence, “all dharmas” means that the appearance exists, and “ultimately without anything whatsoever” means that in reality there is nothing. This case of appearance existing while in reality there is nothing (illusion) is called empty.

[If these two words are viewed as dependent on each other, one suddenly sees their wonder. What is called empty: viewing emptiness through illusory existence, it is named true emptiness. What is called existence: the illusory existence that is originally nothing, it is named wondrous existence. Because of true emptiness, the mind is not annihilated; because of wondrous existence, states are unborn. Since states are unborn, what can the mind grasp? Since the mind grasps nothing, where can deluded thoughts abide? If deluded thoughts do not abide, with what mind will one grasp states? States are themselves illusory; with what states will they entangle the mind? Here the mind simply does not grasp states, and the mind is not annihilated; states do not entangle the mind, and states are of themselves thus. Mind and states thus, in what is one not happy? This is what is meant by “the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states; if the states before it are not, the mind too is not.”]

These two words “empty” and “illusory” should be viewed in the light of each other, and then one suddenly sees their wonder. What is called empty is viewing the substance as originally empty through the appearance of illusory existence (this is named “true emptiness”). What is called existence is the illusory existence that is originally nothing (this is named “wondrous existence”). Because of true emptiness, the mind is not annihilated; because of wondrous existence, states are unborn. Since states are unborn, what can the mind grasp? Since the mind grasps nothing, where can deluded thoughts abide? If deluded thoughts do not abide, with what mind will one grasp states? States are themselves illusory; with what states will they entangle the mind? The mind simply does not grasp states, and the mind is not annihilated; states do not entangle the mind, and states are of themselves thus. Mind and states thus, the two not disturbing each other, in what is one not happy? This is what is meant by “the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states; if the states before it are not, the mind too is not.”

[Mind and states thus] The term “thus” (rúrú) usually describes that which does not change and is not different. Here “thus” means that mind and states each go their own way, without disturbing or entangling each other. [The mind is originally unborn but exists because of states; if the states before it are not, the mind too is not] This is the transmission verse of the Buddha Visvabhu (the third of the seven Buddhas of the past): “Borrowing the four great elements, one takes them for a body; the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states. If the states before it are not, the mind too is not; offense and merit are like illusions, arising and ceasing as well.”

[But simply see through the illusory and unreal, and it is named “as if not”; while the spirit-mind shines alone and deluded mind suddenly rests, and it is named “also not.” What is not is deluded mind; how could it be that the true mind is utterly not! What is deluded mind? That which clings to states and does not melt away. What is true mind? That which does not grasp the marks of body, mind, and states, which is clearly and constantly aware, spiritual and still-illumining. Using the mind thus, what hindrance is there? Hence it is said: “The self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharma. Not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. The non-illusory does not even arise — how can illusory dharmas stand?” And as it is said: “States and conditions have no good or ugly; good and ugly arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcefully name them, from what do love and hate arise?”]

In the line “if the states before it are not, the mind too is not,” one sees through the states before one as illusory and unreal, and so it is named “as if not”; while the spirit-mind shines alone and deluded mind suddenly rests, and so it is named “also not.” What is called “not” means that deluded mind is not; how could it mean that even the true mind is not! What is deluded mind? That which clings to states and does not melt away is deluded mind. What is true mind? That which does not grasp the marks of body, mind, and states, which is clearly and constantly aware, spiritual and still-illumining, is true mind. Using the mind thus (using the true mind), what hindrance is there in states? Hence the Surangama Sutra says: “The self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharma. Not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. The non-illusory does not even arise — how can illusory dharmas stand?” And it is just as the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, Daoxin, said: “States and conditions have no good or ugly; good and ugly arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcefully name them, from what do love and hate arise?”
[The self-mind grasps the self-mind] The Surangama Sutra says:
“When knowing and seeing set up a knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa, taintless and truly pure.”

[If thus the feelings do not attach to things, how can things obstruct a man? Since things cannot obstruct a man, how does a man obstruct things? The reason worldly men cannot be free is only that they do not understand that mind and states are unborn and illusory and unreal. If one understands that a single thought is unborn and like an illusion, then all suffering and joy, care and calamity, gain and loss, love and hate, grasping and rejecting, melt away like ice on the spot. Hence it is said: “Knowing the illusory, one is at once free, without using expedients; free of the illusory, one is at once awake, and there are no stages either.” This is what is meant by “a single thought arrives at the Buddha’s home at once”; it is no idle word.]

In this way, so long as the feelings do not attach to things, how can things obstruct a man? Since things cannot obstruct a man, how does a man obstruct things? The reason worldly men cannot be free is only that they do not understand that mind and states are both unborn (originally non-existent) and illusory and unreal. If one understands that a single thought is unborn and like an illusion, then all suffering and joy, care and calamity, gain and loss, love and hate, grasping and rejecting, melt away like ice on the spot. Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing the illusory, one is at once free, without using expedients; free of the illusory, one is at once awake, and there are no stages either.” This is what is meant by “a single thought arrives at the Buddha’s home at once”; it is no idle word.

[You need only contemplate the place where all deluded thoughts arise and cease, the place where all states arise and cease: all of it is illusory and unreal. Then the mind of itself will not run after states, and states of themselves will not entangle the mind. Coming and going, meeting conditions, a single thought is empty and bright, spirit-like and illumining alone, seeing the body and mind before one as illusory and magical, as the moon in water, as an image in a mirror, as a cloud in the sky, as a mirage and a shimmering haze. Holding the adamantine eye thus, do not move again; let all states come as they will — touched, they vanish at once. Whatever deluded mind there be, one glance and it is gone. Using the mind thus, what deluded mind is there to trouble oneself? What deluded state is there that can entangle the mind?]

You need only contemplate the place where all deluded thoughts arise and cease, the place where all states arise and cease: all of it is illusory and unreal. Then the mind of itself will not run after states, and states of themselves will not entangle the mind. Coming and going, meeting conditions, a single thought is empty and bright, spirit-like and illumining alone, seeing the body and mind before one as illusory and magical, as the moon in water, as an image in a mirror, as a cloud in the sky, as a mirage and a shimmering haze. Holding the adamantine eye thus, do not move again; let all states come as they will — touched, they vanish at once. Whatever deluded mind there be, one glance and it is gone. Using the mind thus, what deluded mind is there to trouble oneself? What deluded state is there that can entangle the mind?

[Shimmering haze] In full, “the horse of the wilds” (yěmǎ): a vapor or a haze of dust that appears far off in the desert or the open plain under the heat — an illusion. When one draws near, the illusion vanishes. [Mirage] A vapor that arises under the blazing sun; from afar it looks like water, and the thirsty long to drink, but in the end it cannot be obtained.
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Attendant Qi on the Boat Bound for Leiyang)

[The Buddhas and patriarchs taught men, amid birth and death, to realize at once the non-birth dharma-patience, and again and again they wondered that men, within the unborn, falsely see birth and ceasing. These words are like telling a man in the marketplace about the events of a dream: the hearer is not one who does not open his eyes wide and pluck up courage, but he has not yet verified it for himself. In short, what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what is seen. The ancients valued actual realization because they wished simply, within the dharmas of birth and death, to see through intimately — there is no other extraordinary place. I once saw a child afraid of ghosts: walking in the night, he fancied that something followed him, and great terror arose. Though his kind mother reasoned with him that originally there was nothing, he did not believe her; he had to wait until he himself believed beyond doubt before he stopped. If he came of himself to the place of no doubt, then even if a ghost were sent to frighten him, he would laugh and let it go.]

The Buddhas and patriarchs taught men, amid birth and death, to realize at once the non-birth dharma-patience. And again and again they sighed over why men, within the unborn (the originally unborn), falsely see birth and ceasing. Those who hear these words cannot but be moved and stirred, yet they have not verified them for themselves; it is just like telling a man on the street about some strange event in a dream — it is truly hard to believe. In short, the principle that is spoken of, that “birth is yet non-birth,” is not what they have ever heard before; and even what they have heard is not what they have seen with their own eyes. Hence it is hard truly to believe. The ancients esteemed those who actually realized the unborn dharma because they wished simply, within the dharmas of birth and death, to see through intimately with their own eyes — there is no other extraordinary place. I once saw a child afraid of ghosts: often, walking alone at night, he always felt that something followed behind him, and was terribly frightened. Though his kind mother reasoned well with him that there was originally nothing following him, he would not believe it. He had to wait until he had verified it himself and truly believed there was nothing, and knew it was all the working of his own mind, his own frightening of himself, before he would no longer feel that something followed him at night. If he had come to the place of complete and undoubting belief in “no ghost follows me,” then even if someone dressed up as a ghost and followed behind him to frighten him, he would laugh it off.

[Non-birth dharma-patience] In brief, non-birth patience: true wisdom resting securely upon the principle of true suchness, which is neither arising nor ceasing. “Neither arising nor ceasing” means: all dharmas are like things in a dream — originally unborn, and therefore also not ceasing. The Diamond Sutra says: “Whatever has marks is false and delusive.”

[In former days I traveled on the frontier, and rode by night with a sturdy fellow. Beside the road was a stone; the horse suddenly saw it and was greatly startled, and nearly threw him to the ground. He then reined in the horse, whipped and urged it mightily, and made it walk round the stone several dozen times; then he led it to look closely at the stone for a long while, and only then let it go loose and gallop off. From that time on, the horse was never startled by anything it met. From this I knew that a man who travels the perilous road of birth and death, testing his mind through states as they come, must do the same and only then be done. Therefore the Avatamsaka uses Sudhana to represent realization. The hundred cities he passed through, the many good friends he consulted — even at the mountain of knives and the mass of fire he still hung back and waited to be urged before entering. And when he entered, he truly attained the gate of cool and great liberation. Is this not what is meant by “urging the horse round the stone and making it look closely”?]

In former days, when I traveled on the frontier, I rode by night with a sturdy fellow. Beside the road was a great stone; his horse suddenly saw it, took it for some monstrous beast, and was greatly startled, and nearly threw him to the ground. He then reined in the horse, and whipped and urged it mightily, making it walk several dozen circles round the stone; then he stopped and led the horse to gaze at it closely for a long while, until it knew there was nothing to fear, and only then let the reins go and galloped off. From that time on, that horse was never startled by anything it met. From this I knew that a man who comes and goes on the perilous road of birth and death, testing his mind through states as they come, must do the same and only then be done (urging the horse round the stone, making it look closely, until it no longer doubts or fears and only then stops). Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra uses Sudhana’s fifty-three visits to make clear how actual realization is won. Sudhana passed through more than a hundred cities and consulted many good friends; and when he came to the Brahmin Shantacitta and faced the mountain of knives and the mass of fire, he was still alarmed and doubtful. Only after repeated urging did he dare to enter. And when he entered, he truly attained the gate of cool and great liberation (personally realizing that the mountain of knives and the mass of fire are an illusion). Is this not precisely “urging the horse round the stone and making it look closely,” so as to see through intimately?
[Frontier] A strategic place on the border. [Sudhana’s fifty-three visits] The Avatamsaka Sutra

, “Entering the Dharma Realm,” relates how the youth Sudhana journeyed south in succession and consulted fifty-three good friends. [The mountain of knives and the mass of fire] This is the ninth of Sudhana’s fifty-three visits, his visit to the Brahmin Shantacitta. When Sudhana came before the Brahmin Shantacitta, he saw on all four sides masses of fire, and in their midst a mountain of knives, high and steep beyond measure. The Brahmin Shantacitta climbed this mountain of knives and then threw himself into the great mass of fire. At that time Sudhana bowed to him, stood with palms joined, and said reverently: “Holy One, I have already brought forth the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but I do not know how to learn the bodhisattva’s practices or how to cultivate the bodhisattva’s way. I have heard that you, Holy One, are skilled in instructing, and I beg you to speak for me.” The Brahmin Shantacitta said: “Good man, if you can now climb this mountain of knives and throw yourself into the mass of fire, then all the bodhisattva’s practices will be purified.” Sudhana’s mind gave rise to doubt: “If I throw myself in, will I not lose my life? Can it be that a demon has taken the form of a bodhisattva to lure me into the evil paths and obstruct my study?” So he was frightened beyond measure. At that time ten thousand great Brahma kings, ten thousand Paranirmita-Vasavartin kings, ten thousand Sunirmita kings, ten thousand Tushita kings, ten thousand Yama kings, ten thousand Shakra kings (lords of the Trayastrimsha heaven), ten thousand naga kings, ten thousand yaksha kings, ten thousand gandharva kings, ten thousand asura kings, ten thousand garuda kings, ten thousand kinnara kings, and measureless gods of the desire realm appeared one after another, crying out in the air, telling Sudhana not to doubt, and testifying for him that the Brahmin Shantacitta was a great good friend. Only after the gods had urged him in turn did Sudhana give rise to faith. “At that time the youth Sudhana, hearing all these various teachings, was greatly delighted, and leaped for joy beyond measure. Before the Brahmin he gave rise to the thought that this was a true good friend. Bowing his head to his feet, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke thus: ‘Toward the great holy good friend I gave rise to disbelief and harbored doubt. I pray only that the Holy One permit me to repent my fault.’ Then the Brahmin spoke a verse for Sudhana: ‘If there are bodhisattvas who follow a good friend’s teaching, without any doubt or fear, abiding with a mind unmoved, they shall surely attain the Buddhas’ natural wisdom, subdue Mara, sit at the place of enlightenment, and broadly save beings beyond measure.’ At that time Sudhana at once climbed the mountain of knives and threw himself into the mass of fire. Before he reached the middle, he attained the bodhisattva’s samādhi of good abiding; and the moment he touched the flames, he attained the bodhisattva’s samādhi of serene bliss and spiritual power.”
[Seen from this, the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other strong point at all; they were simply men who could look closely at the marks of the world
(the world)

. What worldly men dread — is it not birth and death and calamity? Yet the Buddhas and patriarchs wish to make men realize non-birth patience amid these very things, and moreover declare plainly that within the unborn one falsely sees birth and ceasing. Ah! What does this really mean? If one does not look closely until one comes of oneself to the place of no doubt, then in my view, though the compassionate Honored One reason with one well, one will hardly escape dread.]

Seen from this, the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other strong point at all; they were simply able to see clearly that the marks of the world are illusory, and in the midst of what is so plainly birth and ceasing to see only non-birth. What worldly men dread is nothing but birth and death and calamity. Yet the Buddhas and patriarchs wish to make men actually realize non-birth dharma-patience amid birth and death and calamity, and moreover declare plainly: living beings, within the utterly still and unborn, falsely see birth and ceasing. Ah! What does this really point to? If one does not look closely with one’s own eyes until one comes to the place of no doubt, then in my view, though the greatly compassionate World-Honored One instruct one earnestly, when faced with the calamity of birth and death one will probably hardly escape dread.

[Of late, because I spread the Dharma, I met with calamity: it reached even to the sage’s anger, like thunder on a bright day, at which hearers stopped their ears. From the time I was arrested until I came out, more than two hundred days, I passed through bitter things beyond all words. From first to last, I looked within and found that a single thought of joy was not in the least diminished from former days, and those who saw it were all astonished, taking it for something quite out of the ordinary. Yet the calamity of birth and death — others were astonished on my account; and when they saw that my joy was not diminished, they were astonished again. I am not astonished at what astonishes them, while they are astonished at what does not astonish me; perhaps there is a Way in it!]

Of late, because I spread the Dharma, I met with persecution, and it reached even to the sage’s (the emperor’s) anger (the Master, being slandered for spreading the Dharma, enraged the emperor, was arrested and cast into prison, tortured for confession, his life or death unknown), like thunder on a bright day, at which hearers stopped their ears. From the time I was arrested until my exile left the capital, for more than two hundred days, I passed through bitter things beyond all words. From first to last, I looked within and found that a single thought of joy was not in the least diminished from usual, and those who saw it were all greatly astonished. Yet the sudden calamity of birth and death — others were astonished on my account; and when they saw that my joy was not diminished from usual, they were all the more astonished. I am not astonished at the calamity of birth and death at which men are astonished, while men are astonished that I am not astonished; perhaps there is some principle in it!

[Attendant Qi, not grudging three thousand li, came to share my calamity and questioned me in the dark prison. Afterwards, by the grace of the sage’s favor, I was exiled to Lingnan. Qi then accompanied me on the boat, and so I write this in farewell. Alas! The perilous road of birth and death is precisely what men dread; will he not hear of my mind of joy as a thing in a dream? Another day, when I am tested in the field of stillness and cessation, do not take today’s words for the talk of a dream.]

Attendant Qi (an attendant whose surname was Qi) came from three thousand li away to rescue me from danger, and questioned me in the great prison. Before long, by the grace of the emperor’s favor, I was not sentenced to death but exiled to Lingnan. Attendant Qi then accompanied me along the way, as far as the boat bound for Leiyang. Now that he was going back, I wrote these words in farewell. Alas! At the very edge of birth and death — this is precisely what men dread. Yet to hear that I, my body suffering cruel punishment and facing death, had a mind of joy not in the least diminished from usual — is it not like hearing tell of some strange event in a dream? Another day, in the field of stillness and cessation, you will of yourself verify that what I have said is true speech, and will not take today’s words for the talk of a dream.

[Attendant] One who waits at the side of a master or elder, obeying his commands and serving him. [Field of stillness and cessation] The state of realizing non-birth dharma-patience — delusion exhausted and the real revealed, stillness and cessation manifest before one.
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Seat-Master Miaozhan)
To let no single thought slip past is true cultivation; to see through every single thought is real awakening.

[To let no single thought slip past] Do not let any deluded thought slip by (do not be deceived by it). [To see through every single thought] Do not be shrouded by any deluded thought, do not follow its tricks, do not take it for something real.

[From of old the ancients left home for the sake of the great matter of birth and death. Even the Buddhas’ appearing in the world was specially to reveal this matter and nothing more. It is not that apart from birth and death there is a separate Buddhadharma, nor that apart from the Buddhadharma there is a separate birth and death. It is as said: deluded, birth and death begin; awakened, the wheel of rebirth ceases. From this one knows that the ancients’ investigation and seeking was only to get to the bottom of things and seek the ultimate at the head of the road of birth and death; it was not that apart from this, in paper, ink, and letters, or in the three vehicles and twelve teachings, there was something extraordinary to be made of it.]

From of old the ancients left home for the sake of the great matter of escaping birth and death. Even the Buddhas’ appearing in the world was specially to reveal this matter (escaping birth and death) and nothing more. It is not that apart from the great matter of escaping birth and death there is a separate Buddhadharma, nor that apart from the Buddhadharma there is any separate escaping of birth and death. (This means: the Buddhadharma is precisely about escaping birth and death; only what escapes birth and death is Buddhadharma. The birth and death spoken of here means the birth and death of delimited rebirth and the birth and death of transformation.) It is as said: deluded, birth and death begin; awakened, the wheel of rebirth ceases. (“The wheel of rebirth ceases” is the escape from delimited birth and death. Here Master Hanshan especially stresses escaping delimited birth and death, because this is the cultivator’s urgent task.) From this one knows that the ancients’ investigation and seeking was only to find an ultimate way out at the crucial juncture of birth and death, and not, apart from this, to find something extraordinary in paper, ink, and letters, or in the three vehicles and twelve teachings.

[The great matter of birth and death] The great matter of escaping birth and death. The birth and death spoken of here means the birth and death of delimited rebirth and the birth and death of transformation. [The bottom of things] The details, the root cause. [The twelve teachings] All the sutras and teachings. The content of the teachings is divided into twelve classes altogether, and so they are called the twelve divisions of the teaching, also known as the twelve divisions of the sutras.

[Therefore Bodhidharma came from the West, established nothing in words, and only awakened to his own mind, taking this mind as the root of all the dependent and principal retributions of the ten realms of sages and ordinary beings. Awakening to this mind wholly, one is the supreme Mahāyāna; awakening to it in part, one is of the two vehicles; not awakening to it, one is an ordinary being. If one awakens without keeping it, and realizes without attaining, then one is on the road that goes beyond, transcending sages and ordinary beings and escaping birth and death.]

Therefore Patriarch Bodhidharma came from India (ancient India) and established his guiding principle: establish nothing in words, point directly at the human mind. Cultivation lies only in awakening to one’s own mind, because this mind is the root of all the dependent and principal retributions of the ten dharma realms of sages and ordinary beings. Awakening to this mind wholly, one is the supreme Mahāyāna; awakening to it in part, one is of the two vehicles; not awakening to it, one is an ordinary being. If one awakens without keeping it in mind, and realizes without counting it as an attainment, then one is on the road that goes beyond, transcending sages and ordinary beings and escaping birth and death.

[Establish nothing in words] In Chan, awakening to the Way does not involve words and phrases, but single-mindedly transmits mind to mind by its profound purport; this is called “establishing nothing in words, a separate transmission outside the teachings.” The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source, “Chapter on the World-Honored One,” says: “When the World-Honored One was at the Vulture Peak assembly, he held up a flower before the assembly. At that time the men and gods, a million of them, were all at a loss; only the golden-haired ascetic (Mahākāśyapa) broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the subtle Dharma gate of the mark of reality that is no mark, which establishes nothing in words and is a separate transmission outside the teachings; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.”

[Students in recent times are farther from the sages than ever, and have not seen the ancients’ true conduct of practice — passing through, one by one, the states that appear daily before them and the shore of birth and death. In this very daily use, not departing from a single dharma and not abiding in a single dharma, never lightly letting a thing slip past anywhere: this is true and genuine work. In this very present moment, wherever one sees through, one by one, all the states of sound and form, of adverse and favorable, of love and hate, there is the true gate of awakening. In this very place of awakening, each thing and each dharma is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that the Buddhadharma is only when one listens to a seat-master strike the bell and beat the drum, ascend the flower seat, open his mouth wide and learn the howl of the jackal, or when one inclines the ear, bows the head, shuts the eyes, and dons the robe. Therefore the youth Sudhana journeyed south through a hundred cities and paid respects to good friends as numerous as dust-motes in a Buddha-land, and so awakened to the Dharma gates of liberation in every dust-mote and every Buddha-land.]

Students in recent times are far from the sages, and have not seen the ancients’ true conduct of practice — passing through, one by one, the states that appear daily before them and the shore of birth and death. In this very daily use, not departing from (not avoiding) a single dharma and not abiding in (not clinging to) a single dharma, never lightly letting a thing slip past anywhere: this is true and genuine work. In this very present moment, wherever one sees through, one by one, all the states of sound and form, of adverse and favorable, of love and hate — seeing through to the place where one is not deceived and not turned by them — there is the true gate of awakening. In this very place of awakening, each thing and each matter is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that the Buddhadharma is only when one listens to a preacher of sutras strike the bell and beat the drum, ascend the dharma seat, open his mouth wide and imitate the howl of the jackal (falsely speaking the truth), or when one inclines the ear, bows the head, shuts the eyes, and dons the robe (the motions by which a seat-master draws out and awakens a student). Therefore the youth Sudhana journeyed south through more than a hundred cities and paid respects to good friends as numerous as dust-motes in a Buddha-land, and in practice awakened to the Dharma gates of liberation in every dust-mote and every Buddha-land.
