[Seeing through] Not being entangled and manipulated by the dusts of states. [Each thing] Every single matter, every single item. [Seat-master] One who preaches the sutras and speaks the Dharma. [Flower seat] The lotus seat; here it means the dharma seat from which one preaches the sutras and speaks the Dharma. [Jackal] A kind of fox. “The howl of the jackal” is the counterpart of “the lion’s roar,” used to liken one whose practice has not yet ripened but who falsely speaks the truth. [As numerous as dust-motes in a Buddha-land] A figure for an extremely great number. [Every dust-mote and every Buddha-land] A state spoken of in the Avatamsaka Sutra: within each single dust-mote appear countless Buddha-lands (Buddha realms), and in each Buddha-land there are countless dust-motes, and within each dust-mote again appear countless Buddha-lands, layer upon layer without end. Here “every dust-mote and every Buddha-land” is used to describe an extremely great number.

[Yet of Dharma gates there is no need to speak; but as for good friends, how could there be as many as dust-motes in a Buddha-land? Little does one know that “every Buddha-land and every dust-mote” is simply the deluded thoughts, calculations, and emotional dust of our daily use. If one can, at the place where thought arises and moves in daily use, at the place where the roots of feeling are knotted fast, at the place where love and hate cross and are hard to untie, at the place where the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are hard to wear away, — if at the root’s sorest point one drives in the awl
(same as “pricks”)

and sees through them one by one, passes through them one by one, then this is the true good friend, and on the spot one ascends the supreme Dharma gate of unobstructed freedom and great liberation. Apart from this, what other good friend is there to consult? What more extraordinary Dharma gate is there to enter?]

Yet let us leave the Dharma gates aside; to speak of good friends, how could there be as many of them as dust-motes in a Buddha-land, so many that they cannot be counted? Little does one know that what is called “every Buddha-land and every dust-mote” means the deluded thoughts, calculations, and emotional dust of our daily life. If one can, at the place where thought arises and moves in daily life, at the place where the roots of feeling are knotted fast, at the place where love and hate cross and are hard to untie, at the place where the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are hard to wear away, — if at the root’s sorest point one drives in the awl, sees through them
(as a dream or an illusion)
, and passes through them
(cutting off deluded thoughts)

one by one, then this is your true great good friend, and on the spot you attain the supreme Dharma gate of unobstructed freedom and great liberation. Apart from this, what other good friend is there to consult? What more extraordinary Dharma gate is there to enter?
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Chan Man Zhenyu)

[The Chan man Zhenyu was born in Luling. He abandoned wife and children and left home, delighting in the practice of remoteness, his aspiration set on the famous mountains, to consult good friends. The illusory man, carried astray to Linghai by illusory karma, was thus visited by the Chan man. A short while ago he took leave to go to Putuo to pay respects to Master Daguan, who gave him the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu; and again he brought it here to Wuyang.]

The Chan man Zhenyu (this Chan man was named Zhenyu) was born in Luling; he abandoned wife and children and left home, delighting in the practice of distant wandering, and set his resolve to travel all the famous mountains of the world and pay respects to the good friends. The illusory man (Master Hanshan’s name for himself), because the illusory karma of his own transformation carried him into exile at Linghai, was thus visited by the Chan man. Before long he took leave to go to Putuo to pay respects to Master Daguan (that is, the Venerable Zibai, who often taught people with the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu), who gave him the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu; and again he brought this verse to Wuyang (Guangzhou) to seek instruction from me.

[Linghai] The region of Guangdong and Guangxi. Its land leans north upon the Five Ranges and faces south upon the South Sea; hence the name “Linghai.” [The verse of the Buddha Visvabhu] The Buddha Visvabhu is the third of the seven Buddhas of the past. The verse of the Buddha Visvabhu runs: “Borrowing the four great elements, one takes them for a body; the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states. If the states before it are not, the mind too is not; offense and merit are like illusions, arising and ceasing as well.” This means: body, mind, and world are all illusory.

[The illusory man, in the field of illusion, performs illusory Buddha-work, opens the assembly of the illusory, and speaks the illusory Dharma gate. The Chan man bowed and sought instruction, and the illusory man, relying on the samādhi of illusion, spoke for him of all dharmas as states of illusion and dream, and instructed him, saying:]

The illusory man (I, Master Hanshan), in the field of illusion, performs illusory Buddha-work, instructs the assembly of the illusory, and speaks the illusory Dharma gate. The Chan man bowed and sought teaching; and so the illusory man, relying on the samādhi of illusion that the World-Honored One sets forth in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, explained for him that all dharmas are states of illusion and dream, and instructed him, saying:

[Excellent, son of the Buddha! You should consider it well. All Buddhas manifest by the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate by the power of illusion; all of the two vehicles advance toward stillness by the power of illusion; all non-Buddhists fall into confusion by the power of illusion; all living beings undergo birth and death by the power of illusion. And as for the heavenly palaces and pure lands, they are established by the power of illusion; the jeweled groves and precious trees flourish by the power of illusion; the iron beds and copper pillars are furnished by the power of illusion; the cauldrons of boiling water and the furnaces of coals seethe by the power of illusion; the scaled, the shelled, the feathered, and the furred fly and dive by the power of illusion; the crawling, the wriggling, the shelled, and the winged move and rest by the power of illusion. Even to the utmost, what the Buddhas of the three ages have realized and what the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted is nowhere beyond this samādhi of the illusory net. How could the Chan man escape it?]

Excellent, son of the Buddha! You should consider it well. All Buddhas manifest by the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate by the power of illusion; all of the two vehicles advance toward stillness by the power of illusion; all non-Buddhists fall into confusion by the power of illusion; all living beings undergo birth and death by the power of illusion. As for the heavenly palaces and pure lands, they are all established by the power of illusion. The jeweled groves and precious trees all flourish by the power of illusion; the iron beds and copper pillars are all furnished by the power of illusion; the cauldrons of boiling water and the furnaces of coals all seethe by the power of illusion; the scaled, the shelled, the feathered, and the furred all fly and dive by the power of illusion; the crawling, the wriggling, the shelled, and the winged all move and rest by the power of illusion. Even to the utmost, what the Buddhas of the three ages have realized and what the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted is nowhere beyond this samādhi of the illusory net. How could the Chan man be outside the illusory net?

[Try to consider carefully: for what cause do you fall into birth and death? For what cause do you enter a mother’s womb? For what cause are you drowned in the entanglement of craving? For what cause do you wish to escape the sinking? For what cause do you set out and cross beyond the region? For what cause do you consult good friends? For what cause do you tread famous mountains and climb blessed lands, pass through the thicket of the assembly and enter the community of the bound? This year the South Sea, next year Mount Wutai, the year after Mount Emei — you would travel all within the realm, and though you pass through dust-mote kalpas and exhaust the dust-mote lands of the ten directions, serving all the great good friends of the ten directions, it is all nowhere beyond the doorway of illusion; it is not the ultimate and true place.]
